newsitem.title: USA: U.S. condemns use of force by Serbian police.
newsitem.headline: U.S. condemns use of force by Serbian police.

text.p: The United States on Monday condemned what it called "the most serious use of force" against demonstrators in Belgrade over the weekend and urged Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to exercise restraint.
"The United States strongly condemns the violence by the Serbian police against the demonstrators who by all accounts have demonstrated peacefully" State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"We call on the Serb police and the Serb authorities led by President Milosevic to exercise restraint in the streets of Belgrade," Burns told a news briefing.

At least 100 people were reported injured in the clashes. Opposition supporters have been protesting daily since Serbian authorities cancelled results of Nov. 17 local elections in which the opposition Zajedno coalition claimed victory.
Burns said the government action "will only further Serbia's isolation (and) deepen the political crisis in Belgrade. This is an extremely discouraging set of events."
He said that after Sunday's use by Serb police of batons and water cannons on protesters demanding democratic changes in Belgrade, police had used further "brutal force" on Monday.

U.S. charge d'affaires Richard Miles met Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic on Monday morning "to condemn the police action and to call upon the Serbian government officially to refrain from using police force in the streets of Belgrade."
Burns said the diplomat had also met an opposition leader, Vuk Draskovic, to "express our support for the opposition's track record of peaceful protest and to counsel restraint on all sides."

Burns said an off-duty American marine employed to guard the U.S. embassy in Belgrade who was caught up in the violence had been beaten by police. He said the marine, who was not named, was not seriously hurt and was back at work.
Despite the strong words, Burns gave no sign the United States planned any new action against Milosevic. "I think it's a little bit difficult for the United States to get much tougher," he said.

He said existing U.S. political and financial sanctions against Belgrade should not be underestimated, but that it would be difficult to get U.N. Security Council consensus to reimpose previous full trade sanctions on Serbia.

Turning to Bosnia, Burns condemned statements attributed in a Greek newspaper interview to former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic, saying they violated a pledge he had given last July to step down from public life.

The U.S. spokesman described as outrageous comments reported on Sunday by the newspaper Eleftheros Typos that the 1995 Dayton peace accord on Bosnia was merely a truce and that the Serbs might go back to war.

Karadzic "has violated his agreement not to appear in public", Burns said, adding that at the meeting between Miles and Milutinovic, the U.S. diplomat had reminded Belgrade "of its obligation to make sure that Mr Karadzic stays in line".
